1185: Scaling Smarter in the AI Era | Sarah Riley, CFO, dbt Labs
1185: Scaling Smarter in the AI Era | Sarah Riley, CFO, dbt Labs
When the pandemic began reshaping the world in early 2020, Sarah Riley was helping guide finance at Zoom through an unprecedented surge in demand. “You could see the volume of Zoom almost spiking up by the regions that were going into shutdown,” Riley tells us. What followed was unlike anything most software companies had experienced before. During her four years at Zoom, the company expanded from roughly $200 million in ARR to $4 billion, Riley tells us. At one point, Zoom spent nearly half a billion dollars on AWS infrastructure costs it had not anticipated, she explains.
Read More
For Riley, the experience fundamentally reshaped how she viewed finance leadership. Rather than becoming fixated on gross margin guidance or traditional planning cycles, she says the finance team had to continually reevaluate the “strategic heart” of the business as Zoom evolved from an enterprise software company into a platform supporting schools, consumers, and businesses worldwide. “Forecasting and discipline comes second” in moments of extraordinary change, Riley tells us.
That mindset now informs her role as CFO of dbt Labs, where she oversees finance, accounting, and data operations while helping guide the company through its merger with Fivetran. Riley says today’s defining challenge for software businesses is balancing legacy operating models with the realities of AI-driven transformation. “You need to balance that with how do we make sure that we’re investing aggressively enough in capturing what our user base is turning into,” she tells us.

CFOTL: Let’s find out about dbt Labs and this opportunity. You joined as a senior finance person, but within two years you were in the CFO office. It seems like a perfect match. Tell us about DBT first. What’s the company about today?
Riley: DBT is an open-source data infrastructure company. If you talked to our CEO when he started the company nine years ago, his ethos was really about taking software engineering best practices that make code bases organized, high velocity, and easy to govern, and bringing those principles to data teams. Historically, data teams were running these spaghetti code bases that were difficult to manage. We’ve all had the experience of getting an opaque number from a data partner and asking, “Can you help me trace this back to the source?” and finding that incredibly difficult.
Read More
When I joined dbt, the company had very little revenue — I think below $15 million in ARR — but there were already tens of thousands of companies using the open-source product. That told me the company was doing something special that really resonated with data developers. Since then, the platform has evolved into something much more robust that helps organizations govern data cross-platform at scale. In a world where CIOs and chief data officers are deeply focused on ensuring data quality doesn’t become a barrier to AI adoption, that’s become an increasingly important area of infrastructure.
CFOTL: Can we ask about the merger? I know there was a major announcement last year.
Riley: Last October, dbt signed a definitive agreement to merge with Fivetran, and we’re deeply excited about it. DBT and Fivetran have both become best-of-breed midsize players in the data platform space, and together the combined company becomes the third-largest standalone data platform company in the world behind Databricks and Snowflake.
It’s been a fascinating transaction to work on because the companies share so much common ground. Both organizations grew up at roughly the same time and both have very similar philosophies around being platform agnostic and supporting the user. It really felt like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to bring together two companies with such strong alignment.
CFOTL: Tell us something about your mindset when it comes to performance and what really drives performance in this business.
Riley: In addition to managing finance and accounting, I also manage our data team, so we spend a lot of time thinking about how to leverage our platform to create a truly data-driven environment internally. We’re very focused on product analytics, go-to-market analytics, and having absolute clarity around the KPIs that matter across every area of the business.
We invest early in building strong data literacy and accountability among our executives so that when we review financials, we’re reviewing them in tandem with business KPIs. Everyone understands that the investments we make are intended to drive specific outcomes. Every couple of quarters we revisit those assumptions to make sure we’re still focused on the right things. It’s really a hand-in-hand finance and data effort.
CFOTL: Before the results show up, what inputs matter most?
Riley: For us, the business KPIs are really the leading indicators. We focus heavily on the health and growth of our open-source community because that effectively becomes the top of our funnel. We’re constantly evaluating how customers are using new features, how that drives adoption of the platform product, and how we can make the experience even more compelling.
That thinking flows into our go-to-market planning as well. Do we have the right sellers? Do we have the right resources allocated? Do we have the right “chess pieces” on the board to hit our goals? Then we reflect back and ask whether those assumptions produced the financial profile we expected.
CFOTL: Can you share a little more about your insight into the customer experience and your efforts to understand it?
Riley: We try to be thoughtful about customer privacy, especially on the open-source side, so we don’t collect an excessive amount of data there. But we absolutely monitor feature consumption among customers who move onto the platform. We want to understand what they find valuable and what drives conversion.
For many open-source companies, the community is viewed primarily as a way to drive adoption or contribute to the engineering ecosystem. But from a finance perspective, I think you have to think about open source fundamentally as a distribution method. Our North Star is making sure that the commercial platform is valuable enough that it becomes an obvious next step for users. DBT’s open-source community is still growing about 70% year-over-year at scale, with more than 100,000 companies on the platform, so the opportunity is significant.

At Aledade, CFO Jessica Somers is helping finance navigate a business where investment decisions can take years to fully reveal their value.The technology-driven, physician-led company works with more than 3,000 primary care practices and touches more than 3.6 million patients, using data and technology to support proactive, preventive care. Its value-based model also creates an unusual finance challenge: connecting better patient outcomes with healthcare savings and, ultimately, financial performance.That long-term orientation shapes how Somers approaches capital allocation. Aledade has built its own technology platform rather than relying on another company’s roadmap, reflecting what Somers describes as a desire to “control our destiny.” Today, that same thinking is influencing the company’s approach to AI.Rather than viewing investments as isolated projects to be stack-ranked strictly by ROI, Somers wants leaders to understand how different investments interact and compound. That became particularly important as Aledade weighed continued progress toward profitability against the opportunity to make larger AI investments. The result was a willingness to make bigger bets where leadership saw the potential to extend the company’s advantage.Somers’ perspective is shaped by an earlier career in investment banking, private equity, and corporate development. Moving from advising on transactions to operating inside the businesses themselves taught her that financial results reflect countless everyday decisions—and that finance creates the most value when it deeply understands the business behind the numbers.Her agenda now extends that philosophy to AI: not simply using technology to make finance faster, but reimagining work so the team has greater capacity for judgment, insight, and strategic partnership.

At a glance
 The dbt Labs team overcame scalability and data accuracy issues by transitioning from Google Sheets to Pigment.
 They needed a flexible solution that could scale effectively with a fast-changing business in a fast-changing macro environment.
 They chose Pigment, impressed by its integration and scenario analysis capabilities.
Founded in 2016, dbt Labs is a tech company based in Philadelphia and the creator of dbt (data build tool), an open-source tool that enables data analysts and engineers to manage data in their warehouses more efficiently and collaboratively.
> “I’ve done several EPM implementations over the last decade of my career, and every time we’ve had a solution that wasn’t nimble enough to meet the business needs. That’s what pushed us to Pigment. Being a data transformation company, our ethos of bringing data together really aligns to what Pigment does.”
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
Retiring the spreadsheet
Before Pigment, the finance team were being held back by their use of spreadsheets.
> "We were doing everything on Google Sheets, and the difficulty in managing the data flow, it fell out of being current/accurate really quickly, it was really manual, and with the pace of growth the team was experiencing, it wasn’t going to scale for our financial planning needs."
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
Why Pigment?
dbt Labs needed an effective solution that would not only accommodate their growing needs but also streamline their operations, particularly in workforce planning. Pigment stood out for the following reasons:
 Scalability: Being a growing business, dbt Labs required a tool that could grow along with it. Pigment provided a solution that removed the limitations they were experiencing with Google Sheets.
 Real-time data: One of the standout offerings of Pigment was the ability to track the progress of different teams in real-time, ensuring interventions could be made where required.
 Data accuracy: The complexities of managing multiple spreadsheets often give rise to errors. Pigment eliminated this risk with an all-in-one, automated platform.
 Scenario planning: dbt Labs needed the ability to rapidly spin up and explore business scenarios.
> “The ability to take a baseline and play through multiple different scenarios and get back to your executive teams with the implications quickly is really important. It’s an exciting time to be in finance, because we’re offering more value.”
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
The result
Before Pigment, updating Google Sheets took days of team members’ time just to analyze progress against the plan. Now, dbt Labs has seamless data flow, particularly around workforce planning. That means they’re able to check in before the end of quarter to help teams hit their goals, rather than waiting until they’re near the finish line.

Founded in 2016, dbt Labs is a tech company based in Philadelphia and the creator of dbt (data build tool), an open-source tool that enables data analysts and engineers to manage data in their warehouses more efficiently and collaboratively.
> “I’ve done several EPM implementations over the last decade of my career, and every time we’ve had a solution that wasn’t nimble enough to meet the business needs. That’s what pushed us to Pigment. Being a data transformation company, our ethos of bringing data together really aligns to what Pigment does.”
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
Retiring the spreadsheet
Before Pigment, the finance team were being held back by their use of spreadsheets.
> "We were doing everything on Google Sheets, and the difficulty in managing the data flow, it fell out of being current/accurate really quickly, it was really manual, and with the pace of growth the team was experiencing, it wasn’t going to scale for our financial planning needs."
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
Why Pigment?
dbt Labs needed an effective solution that would not only accommodate their growing needs but also streamline their operations, particularly in workforce planning. Pigment stood out for the following reasons:
 Scalability: Being a growing business, dbt Labs required a tool that could grow along with it. Pigment provided a solution that removed the limitations they were experiencing with Google Sheets.
 Real-time data: One of the standout offerings of Pigment was the ability to track the progress of different teams in real-time, ensuring interventions could be made where required.
 Data accuracy: The complexities of managing multiple spreadsheets often give rise to errors. Pigment eliminated this risk with an all-in-one, automated platform.
 Scenario planning: dbt Labs needed the ability to rapidly spin up and explore business scenarios.
> “The ability to take a baseline and play through multiple different scenarios and get back to your executive teams with the implications quickly is really important. It’s an exciting time to be in finance, because we’re offering more value.”
>
> Sarah Riley, Head of Finance & Strategy, dbt Labs
The result
Before Pigment, updating Google Sheets took days of team members’ time just to analyze progress against the plan. Now, dbt Labs has seamless data flow, particularly around workforce planning. That means they’re able to check in before the end of quarter to help teams hit their goals, rather than waiting until they’re near the finish line.

dbt Labs is on a mission to help analysts create and disseminate organizational knowledge. dbt Labs pioneered the practice of analytics engineering, built the primary tool in the analytics engineering toolbox–dbt—and has been fortunate to see a fantastic community coalesce around the analytics engineering workflow. Today there are 6000+ companies using dbt; 17,000+ folks in the dbt Slack community; and 1,000+ dbt Cloud customers.

“We didn’t set out with an explicit goal to become a VC-backed company. We were extremely happy just running a profitable small business that did good work for good people if that’s what made the most sense. Accepting venture money means giving up a certain amount of control over your long-term trajectory, and we just weren’t sure that we were ready to do that. The investments we made with the Lighter Capital dollars were exactly what gave us the confidence to charge down the VC-backed route, and we’ve never looked back.”

Thinking long-term
dbt Labs, a software and consultancy company founded in 2017, has made remarkable strides since receiving initial funding from Lighter Capital in 2019. The company’s long-term objective is to improve the way data analysts work through higher-leverage tooling. dbt Labs’ professional services team, composed of analytics engineers, supports companies with data organization via modeling. The team builds and maintains dbt, an open-source data modeling tool used by over 5,000 companies today. dbt Labs’s clients include JetBlue Airways, Casper, Invision, Gitlab, and Hubspot, to name a few.
Financing success
On June 30, 2021, dbt Labs announced its third major investment round since early 2020. The round was co-led by Altimeter, as well as prior investors Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz. It is rare to see not only a series A, but a series B and C in a 16 month time span. The company’s novel approach to data transformation is used by companies ranging from early stage startups to blue-chip Fortune 500 companies.
Growing traction
dbt has seen widespread and growing traction. Snowflake, a cloud computing-based data warehousing company, recently qualified dbt as a Validated Technology, and over 5,000 companies use dbt as part of their weekly analytics engineering workflow.
The short timeframe between dbt Lab’s Series A, Series B, and now Series C signals strong investor confidence. As more organizations see the need to streamline and leverage their data, dbt will likely see growing demand for its services. Snowflake’s recent IPO, Databricks’ rapid growth, and the multi-billion-dollar acquisitions from Google and Salesforce all indicate a large market opportunity.
Getting started with Lighter Capital
In 2019, dbt Labs reached out to Lighter Capital for funding. Lighter Capital helps fund companies through a revenue-based financing solution that scales with a business‘s growth, allowing entrepreneurs to focus on their company’s development without giving up equity, personal guarantees, or board seats.
The funding from Lighter Capital allowed dbt Labs to build a world-class team of engineers while expanding its product offering. Lighter Capital’s funding gave dbt Labs the necessary time to develop its growth and funding paths.
dbt Labs CEO, Tristan Handy, considers bootstrapping, and later raising capital from Lighter, to be a core part of the company’s success.
“We didn’t set out with an explicit goal to become a VC-backed company,” said Handy. “We were extremely happy just running a profitable small business that did good work for good people if that’s what made the most sense. Accepting venture money means giving up a certain amount of control over your long-term trajectory, and we just weren’t sure that we were ready to do that. The investments we made with the Lighter Capital dollars were exactly what gave us the confidence to charge down the VC-backed route, and we’ve never looked back.”
Thinking big
The $150m in Series C financing from Altimeter and existing partners Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz will allow dbt Labs to further build out an extraordinary team of engineers and expand the breadth dbt’s product suite. “Cash gives us time, and time gives us the freedom to think big,” said Handy.

Sarah Jane Friar OBE (born 24 December 1972) is a British-Irish and American business executive, who has been the chief financial officer (CFO) of OpenAI since June 2024. She was the chief executive officer of American technology company Nextdoor from 2018 to 2024 and the CFO of Block, Inc. (formerly Square, Inc.) from 2012 to 2018.
Early life
[edit]
[personal detail removed]eland. She attended Strabane Grammar School. Friar won a scholarship from the accounting firm Arthur Andersen after entering a competition; she then worked there for a year before pursuing engineering studies at University of Oxford. She studied metallurgy, economics, and management at Oxford, and then completed an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business where she was an Arjay Miller scholar. Friar interned at Ashanti Goldfields in 1990s, during which she was assigned to work at a gold mine in Ghana.
Career
[edit]
Friar worked as an analyst for McKinsey & Company in South Africa, a managing director in equity research at Goldman Sachs, and a senior vice president of finance and strategy at Salesforce before becoming chief financial officer at Square in 2012. She then joined Nextdoor, a hyperlocal social networking service for neighborhoods, as CEO in 2018. Friar led the company public through a special-purpose acquisition company in 2021. Nextdoor announced Friar would step down as CEO in mid-2024. In June 2024, she joined OpenAI, the artificial intelligence research organization that develops ChatGPT, as its first CFO.
Friar is on the boards of Walmart and ConsenSys, and previously sat on the boards of Slack Technologies and New Relic's boards. She also co-chairs Stanford's Digital Economy Lab and runs Ladies Who Launch, a non-profit focused on female entrepreneurs that she co-founded.
She received an honorary doctorate from Ulster University in 2018. In 2019, she was granted an Order of the British Empire from Queen Elizabeth II for her commitment to entrepreneurship and financial services.
Personal life
[edit]
Friar is married to David Riley, a former hedge fund partner. The couple has a daughter and son. She lives in Marin County, California. She was also named on Time "Time (magazine)")'s list of the most influential people in the world in 2026.

What's Rarely Measured Matters Most
1185: Scaling Smarter in the AI Era | Sarah Riley, CFO, dbt Labs
1185: Scaling Smarter in the AI Era | Sarah Riley, CFO, dbt Labs
When the pandemic began reshaping the world in early 2020, Sarah Riley was helping guide finance at Zoom through an unprecedented surge in demand. “You could see the volume of Zoom almost spiking up by the regions that were going into shutdown,” Riley tells us. What followed was unlike anything most software companies had experienced before. During her four years at Zoom, the company expanded from roughly $200 million in ARR to $4 billion, Riley tells us. At one point, Zoom spent nearly half a billion dollars on AWS infrastructure costs it had not anticipated, she explains.
Read More
For Riley, the experience fundamentally reshaped how she viewed finance leadership. Rather than becoming fixated on gross margin guidance or traditional planning cycles, she says the finance team had to continually reevaluate the “strategic heart” of the business as Zoom evolved from an enterprise software company into a platform supporting schools, consumers, and businesses worldwide. “Forecasting and discipline comes second” in moments of extraordinary change, Riley tells us.
That mindset now informs her role as CFO of dbt Labs, where she oversees finance, accounting, and data operations while helping guide the company through its merger with Fivetran. Riley says today’s defining challenge for software businesses is balancing legacy operating models with the realities of AI-driven transformation. “You need to balance that with how do we make sure that we’re investing aggressively enough in capturing what our user base is turning into,” she tells us.

CFOTL: Let’s find out about dbt Labs and this opportunity. You joined as a senior finance person, but within two years you were in the CFO office. It seems like a perfect match. Tell us about DBT first. What’s the company about today?
Riley: DBT is an open-source data infrastructure company. If you talked to our CEO when he started the company nine years ago, his ethos was really about taking software engineering best practices that make code bases organized, high velocity, and easy to govern, and bringing those principles to data teams. Historically, data teams were running these spaghetti code bases that were difficult to manage. We’ve all had the experience of getting an opaque number from a data partner and asking, “Can you help me trace this back to the source?” and finding that incredibly difficult.
Read More
When I joined dbt, the company had very little revenue — I think below $15 million in ARR — but there were already tens of thousands of companies using the open-source product. That told me the company was doing something special that really resonated with data developers. Since then, the platform has evolved into something much more robust that helps organizations govern data cross-platform at scale. In a world where CIOs and chief data officers are deeply focused on ensuring data quality doesn’t become a barrier to AI adoption, that’s become an increasingly important area of infrastructure.
CFOTL: Can we ask about the merger? I know there was a major announcement last year.
Riley: Last October, dbt signed a definitive agreement to merge with Fivetran, and we’re deeply excited about it. DBT and Fivetran have both become best-of-breed midsize players in the data platform space, and together the combined company becomes the third-largest standalone data platform company in the world behind Databricks and Snowflake.
It’s been a fascinating transaction to work on because the companies share so much common ground. Both organizations grew up at roughly the same time and both have very similar philosophies around being platform agnostic and supporting the user. It really felt like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to bring together two companies with such strong alignment.
CFOTL: Tell us something about your mindset when it comes to performance and what really drives performance in this business.
Riley: In addition to managing finance and accounting, I also manage our data team, so we spend a lot of time thinking about how to leverage our platform to create a truly data-driven environment internally. We’re very focused on product analytics, go-to-market analytics, and having absolute clarity around the KPIs that matter across every area of the business.
We invest early in building strong data literacy and accountability among our executives so that when we review financials, we’re reviewing them in tandem with business KPIs. Everyone understands that the investments we make are intended to drive specific outcomes. Every couple of quarters we revisit those assumptions to make sure we’re still focused on the right things. It’s really a hand-in-hand finance and data effort.
CFOTL: Before the results show up, what inputs matter most?
Riley: For us, the business KPIs are really the leading indicators. We focus heavily on the health and growth of our open-source community because that effectively becomes the top of our funnel. We’re constantly evaluating how customers are using new features, how that drives adoption of the platform product, and how we can make the experience even more compelling.
That thinking flows into our go-to-market planning as well. Do we have the right sellers? Do we have the right resources allocated? Do we have the right “chess pieces” on the board to hit our goals? Then we reflect back and ask whether those assumptions produced the financial profile we expected.
CFOTL: Can you share a little more about your insight into the customer experience and your efforts to understand it?
Riley: We try to be thoughtful about customer privacy, especially on the open-source side, so we don’t collect an excessive amount of data there. But we absolutely monitor feature consumption among customers who move onto the platform. We want to understand what they find valuable and what drives conversion.
For many open-source companies, the community is viewed primarily as a way to drive adoption or contribute to the engineering ecosystem. But from a finance perspective, I think you have to think about open source fundamentally as a distribution method. Our North Star is making sure that the commercial platform is valuable enough that it becomes an obvious next step for users. DBT’s open-source community is still growing about 70% year-over-year at scale, with more than 100,000 companies on the platform, so the opportunity is significant.

AI, ISOs & ISVs: The Payments Model Is Shifting
Merchant Sales Podcast
What does the future look like for ISOs as AI, vertical software, and changing payments models reshape the industry? James Shepherd sits down with Brian Abernethy, founder and CEO of Straata, to discuss the opportunities hiding in residuals, interchange optimization, merchant pricing, and the growing role of AI in payments. They also dive into why the ISO and ISV worlds have struggled to work together, whether that relationship could finally change, and why distribution may become one of the biggest advantages ISOs have in an AI-driven market. The episode wraps up with Patti Murphy’s Today in Payments, covering the Durbin Amendment, debit interchange, IRS card payments, Mastercard’s tax case, ACH growth, Checkout.com entering in-person payments, and what’s next for Clover.

1215: Building Finance for the Long Game | Jessica Somers, CFO, Aledade
CFO THOUGHT LEADER
At Aledade, CFO Jessica Somers is helping finance navigate a business where investment decisions can take years to fully reveal their value.The technology-driven, physician-led company works with more than 3,000 primary care practices and touches more than 3.6 million patients, using data and technology to support proactive, preventive care. Its value-based model also creates an unusual finance challenge: connecting better patient outcomes with healthcare savings and, ultimately, financial performance.That long-term orientation shapes how Somers approaches capital allocation. Aledade has built its own technology platform rather than relying on another company’s roadmap, reflecting what Somers describes as a desire to “control our destiny.” Today, that same thinking is influencing the company’s approach to AI.Rather than viewing investments as isolated projects to be stack-ranked strictly by ROI, Somers wants leaders to understand how different investments interact and compound. That became particularly important as Aledade weighed continued progress toward profitability against the opportunity to make larger AI investments. The result was a willingness to make bigger bets where leadership saw the potential to extend the company’s advantage.Somers’ perspective is shaped by an earlier career in investment banking, private equity, and corporate development. Moving from advising on transactions to operating inside the businesses themselves taught her that financial results reflect countless everyday decisions—and that finance creates the most value when it deeply understands the business behind the numbers.Her agenda now extends that philosophy to AI: not simply using technology to make finance faster, but reimagining work so the team has greater capacity for judgment, insight, and strategic partnership.

Biography
Sarah Riley was Chief Financial Officer of dbt Labs from June 2024 to May 2026. LinkedIn now lists her in San Francisco as SVP / Head of FP&A, Corp Dev & Canva Ventures at Canva. A predecessor’s LinkedIn post said she would succeed him as CFO after almost nine years across Okta, Zoom and dbt Labs. Her own post on stepping into the CFO role said she was incredibly excited to take it.
CFO Thought Leader’s May 2026 interview, recorded while she was still CFO, said that during four years at Zoom the company expanded from roughly $200 million in ARR to $4 billion, and that at dbt she oversaw finance, accounting and data operations while helping guide the Fivetran merger. Semistructured’s note on the executive bench said she had helped Okta and Zoom chart their paths through IPO. LinkedIn also lists a Zoom stretch of January 2021–August 2024 and a prior dbt finance role from February 2023 before the CFO title.
She is based in San Francisco. The dbt CFO years were listed on LinkedIn as New York.

How Canva Built a $25+ Billion Company by Solving a Problem Everyone Ignored

How Canva Built a $25+ Billion Company by Solving a Problem Everyone Ignored
Images
Authored by
Team Foxhog India
Date Released
17 July, 2026
Comments
No Comments
Building a great startup isn’t always about creating something entirely new. Sometimes, it’s about making something difficult feel effortless.
When founders think about billion-dollar startups, they often imagine groundbreaking technology, complex artificial intelligence, or revolutionary inventions that completely reshape an industry. While those businesses certainly exist, some of the world’s most valuable companies have grown by solving problems that millions of people quietly accepted as “just the way things are.”
Canva is one of those companies.
Today, Canva serves more than 200 million users worldwide and has become one of the most recognizable software companies in the world. Designers, students, entrepreneurs, marketers, and large enterprises rely on it every day to create presentations, social media posts, marketing materials, and business documents. Yet when Canva first entered the market, professional design software was already dominated by established players with decades of experience.
From the outside, it looked like there wasn’t much room for another design platform.
The founders saw something everyone else overlooked.
The Problem Was Never Design
For years, digital design tools were built for professional designers. They offered extraordinary creative control, but they also required significant time to learn. Small business owners, startup founders, teachers, and content creators often found themselves struggling with software that wasn’t designed for them.
The challenge wasn’t a lack of design software.
The challenge was accessibility.
Millions of people wanted to create high-quality designs but didn’t want to spend months learning complicated tools. They weren’t looking for every advanced feature imaginable. They simply wanted software that allowed them to turn an idea into a polished design within minutes.
That simple observation became Canva’s biggest competitive advantage.
Instead of asking how to build a more powerful design platform, the founders asked how to build a simpler one.
Simple Doesn’t Mean Easy
Making software simple is often far more difficult than adding new features.
Every additional button, menu, and customization option increases complexity. The hardest part of product development isn’t deciding what to build—it’s deciding what not to build.
Canva focused relentlessly on reducing friction. The interface felt intuitive, templates removed the fear of starting from a blank page, and drag-and-drop editing allowed users to create professional-looking designs without prior experience.
This wasn’t an accident.
It was a product philosophy.
The company understood that every minute saved for the customer increased the likelihood they would return.
That focus on usability helped transform Canva from a useful tool into a daily habit for millions of users.
Growth Followed Customer Success
Many startups invest heavily in customer acquisition before perfecting the product. Canva approached growth differently.
Instead of relying solely on aggressive advertising, the company created an experience that encouraged users to share what they built. Every presentation, social media graphic, poster, or invitation became an indirect advertisement for the platform itself.
Word-of-mouth became one of Canva’s strongest marketing channels.
Businesses recommended it to colleagues.
Teachers introduced it to students.
Marketing teams adopted it because collaboration became easier.
The product itself generated awareness.
That kind of growth is difficult to manufacture through advertising alone.
Funding Was a Tool, Not the Strategy
Like many successful startups, Canva raised significant venture capital throughout its journey. Those investments helped the company expand internationally, hire world-class talent, improve infrastructure, and develop new features.
However, funding wasn’t the reason Canva became successful.
The product had already demonstrated clear customer demand.
Investors weren’t funding an idea alone. They were funding measurable adoption, strong retention, and a business that had already proven people were willing to make it part of their everyday workflow.
This distinction matters because founders often mistake funding for validation.
Validation comes from customers.
Funding simply allows validated businesses to grow faster.
The Biggest Lesson for Founders
Many entrepreneurs believe they need to invent something completely new to build a successful company.
Canva proves otherwise.
The company didn’t invent graphic design.
It reinvented the experience of creating it.
Instead of competing on technical complexity, Canva competed on simplicity, accessibility, and speed. Those qualities made professional design available to people who had never considered themselves designers before.
That’s an important reminder for founders.
Innovation doesn’t always mean creating a new market.
Sometimes it means making an existing market dramatically easier to use.
What Foxhog Ventures Believes
At Foxhog Ventures, we often meet founders searching for ideas that sound revolutionary.
While ambition is important, the startups that create lasting value usually begin with a much simpler question:
“What frustrates people every single day?”
The answers are rarely glamorous.
Complicated software.
Slow processes.
Confusing user experiences.
Inefficient workflows.
Founders who solve these problems exceptionally well often build businesses that customers recommend without being asked.
Canva didn’t become successful because it had the most features.
It became successful because it removed unnecessary complexity.
That’s a lesson every startup can learn from.
Final Thoughts
Every successful startup eventually reaches a point where growth appears obvious in hindsight.
Looking back today, Canva feels inevitable.
But its success wasn’t inevitable.
It came from understanding customers better than competitors, simplifying an experience millions of people found frustrating, and staying committed to that vision while larger companies focused elsewhere.
For founders, the takeaway is clear.
Don’t chase complexity because it sounds innovative.
Build products that people genuinely enjoy using.
Because the companies that change industries aren’t always the ones with the biggest ideas.
They’re often the ones that make everyday problems disappear.
At Foxhog Ventures, we believe the strongest businesses aren’t built by adding more. They’re built by understanding what customers truly need—and removing everything they don’t.

Why Canva’s Acquisition Spree Puts Adobe on Notice in Battle for Creative Marketing Tools
McKinsey reports that 92% of marketers use AI for campaign personalization, and companies using AI in sales and marketing see 10-20% higher ROI.
RETAILBOSS and Jeanel Alvarado
∙ Paid
Canva’s latest string of deals from scooping up Affinity’s pro design suite to buying AI powerhouse Leonardo, Mango AI, and most recently Cavalry, makes clear it is no longer content to play in Adobe’s shadow, but is building a full-stack, AI-native creative marketing platform.
Canva acquired MangoAI and Cavalry this week, representing a strategic expansion into professional creative tools and proprietary AI algorithms, positioning the company as a unified alternative to Adobe’s fragmented product suite. With $4 billion in annualized revenue and 265 million users, Canva demonstrates how AI-native platforms are reshaping the creative software market.
What You Need to Know:
 Canva acquired MangoAI (marketing algorithms) and Cavalry (motion design) in early 2026, following Affinity, Leonardo, and MagicBrief purchases
 The company generated $4 billion in annualized revenue in 2025, up 36% year-over-year, with 31 million paid seats
 Canva created a Chief Algorithms Officer role, signaling a shift from licensing AI to building proprietary capabilities
 Adobe’s 30% stock decline in early 2026 reflects market reassessment of legacy software vendors facing AI disruption
 Professional adoption remains the critical test for Canva’s enterprise expansion strategy
Canva announced two acquisitions in early 2025: MangoAI, a marketing-algorithm startup, and Cavalry, a UK-based motion design platform. The deals follow a pattern established with previous purchases of Affinity, Leonardo, and MagicBrief.
The timing is notable. Adobe’s shares declined 30% in early 2026 as investors reassessed software companies facing AI disruption. Canva closed 2025 with $4 billion in annualized revenue, up 36% year-over-year, with more than 31 million paid seats.
What Canva’s Acquisition Pattern Reveals About Market Strategy
When Canva made Affinity free in October 2024, analysts viewed it as a user acquisition tactic. The actual signal was different. Affinity surpassed 5 million downloads within months, demonstrating professional designers were actively seeking alternatives to Adobe’s pricing structure.
The MangoAI acquisition reveals additional strategic depth. Nirmal Govind, former Vice President of Data Science and Engineering at Netflix, joins Canva as its first Chief Algorithms Officer. This newly created role signals Canva is building proprietary algorithmic capabilities rather than relying on third-party AI models.
Cavalry brings immediate enterprise credibility. The platform is used by motion designers at Amazon, Meta, Google, and Netflix. Canva gains enterprise-grade 2D animation capabilities and direct relationships with Fortune 500 creative teams.
Strategic Insight: Canva’s acquisitions target three integration points: professional design tools, AI generation capabilities, and workflow automation. Each purchase fills a specific gap in the creative production pipeline.
How Adobe’s Approach Differs from Canva’s AI Integration
Adobe treated AI as a feature enhancement to existing products. Canva treated it as infrastructure. The difference appears in usage data: Canva’s AI tools have been used more than 24 billion times to generate presentations, transform documents, create videos, and scale content across channels.
Market research supports this approach. McKinsey reports that 92% of marketers use AI for campaign personalization, and companies using AI in sales and marketing see 10-20% higher ROI.

On Monday, creative suite maker Canva announced the dual acquisition of startups Cavalry, which works on animation, and MangoAI, which works on improving ad performance.
U.K.-based Cavalry works on 2D motion animation for different verticals such as advertising, marketing, gaming, and generative art. Canva said that Cavalry’s tooling will add to the existing capabilities of Affinity, Canva’s professional creative editing suite for photos, vectors, and layouts, which it acquired in 2024.
Canva revamped Affinity’s design last year and made it free for all users. The company said that since then, people have downloaded the software over 5 million times. Affinity has the capabilities of photos, vector, and layout editing. With this acquisition, Canva wants to add motion editing to its suite.
“By bringing Cavalry alongside Affinity, we’re closing that [motion editing] gap and unlocking a complete professional suite spanning photo, vector, layout, and now motion editing,” the company said in a blog post. “Together, these tools form the foundation of a full-stack Creative OS for professional work, while preserving the depth and control professional creatives rely on,” it added.
Besides Cavalry, Canva has also acquired stealth startup MangoAI, which was working on building reinforcement learning systems to improve video ad performance, according to its website. Canva said that the startup’s first product helped clients create and launch ads and observe outcomes to improve future campaigns.
MangoAI was built by Nirmal Govind, former Vice President of Data Science & Engineering at Netflix, and Vinith Misra, a former data scientist at Netflix and Roblox. Canva said that Govind will become Canva’s first “chief algorithms officer” and Misra will work on improving Canva’s marketing products.
In January 2025, Canva acquired marketing intelligence startup MagicBrief and later last year, it launched a growth tool called Canva Grow for asset creation and performance measurement.
During a sit-down at Web Summit Qatar earlier this month, Canva co-founder and COO Cliff Obrecht told TechCrunch that Canva Grow is doing “incredibly well,” especially when it comes to creating static content and publishing it to Meta platforms.
“It is quite an early product, but we’ll soon be launching a lot more things around video creation, deploying across multi-platform,” Obrecht said. “So it’s very early, but it’s very much got a very loyal small user base, but a lot of big brands are spending money, and then we’re scaling up massively.”
With the new acquisitions, the company wants to bolster its position as a marketing solution by potentially adding video creation and more granular measurement. Canva closed 2025 at $4 billion in annualized revenue with more than 265 million users and 31 million paid users.

Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'

Getty A woman with long dark hair wearing a black jacket gestures with her hands
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

Introducing Canva AI 2.0: Reimagining how the world creates
April 16, 2026
> We've always believed imagination is the most powerful force in the world. Now, for the first time, it's also the starting point for creation. Powered by the world's first foundation model built for creativity, say hello to Canva AI 2.0.
  
TL;DR:
   Canva is introducing Canva AI 2.0, its most significant product evolution since launching in 2013, transforming Canva into a conversational, agentic platform where teams can go from the spark of an idea to complete, published work in one place.  
   Powered by the Canva Design Model – the world's first foundation model built to understand the structure, hierarchy, and complexity of real-world design – Canva AI 2.0 generates fully layered, editable output from a single prompt, and gets smarter the more you use it.  
   Available today as a research preview, Canva AI 2.0 introduces a new architecture layer spanning conversational design, iterative agentic editing, layered object intelligence, and living memory, alongside six new intelligent workflows: connectors, scheduling, web research, brand intelligence, Sheets AI, and Canva Code 2.0.   
Our mission at Canva has always been to empower the world to design. When we started out a decade ago, that meant bringing complex and fragmented software into one simple, easy-to-use platform where anyone could bring their ideas to life. Today, we’re incredibly proud to be empowering more than a quarter of a billion people every month, and now, we're stepping into our next era
We're incredibly excited to introduce Canva AI 2.0: an entirely new way to create, and the biggest product launch in our history.
Image 3: Canva AI 2.0 hero collage of features
Imagination as the starting point
Rather than starting with a template or a blank page, you can now start with an idea, a goal, a brief, a rough sketch, even an unfinished thought – and work through it in conversation with Canva AI. It assembles designs from individual components with layout, hierarchy, and brand built in from the first output.
Every element remains fully layered and editable, so you can jump in, collaborate, refine, and iterate as your ideas evolve. Ask Canva AI to create a multi-channel campaign plan to launch your latest product, and it instantly generates content in every format, for every channel, on brand by default.
Video 1
What makes Canva AI 2.0 different
Canva AI 2.0 is designed to stay present through the whole creative process. It understands intent, handles complex requests, and takes coordinated action across an entire design – all without interrupting your flow. When you want to take over and edit manually, it steps back until you need it again.
Image 5: Canva AI being used to help make a Canva doc based on a meeting transcript and turn it into a summary with clear next steps
Four key capabilities make this possible:
Conversational design means creation starts with a conversation. Describe an idea, a goal, or a rough structure, and Canva AI generates a fully editable design with layout, hierarchy, and brand from the start, then stays with you throughout the entire process. It maintains context as your ideas evolve and helps you brainstorm, refine, and iterate at every step.
Video 2
Agentic orchestration gives Canva AI access to Canva’s complete design engine, calling the right tools at the right time. Describe a goal, share a sketch, or provide a brief, and Canva AI brings it to life: understanding your intent, selecting the right capabilities, and coordinating them into a complete outcome. Ask it to build anything – from a product launch campaign to a client presentation or a social content series – and it handles everything.
Video 3
With layered object intelligence, everything Canva AI generates is built from scratch using individual, editable objects rather than generating a static or locked flat image. Ask Canva AI to change something, and only that changes. Swap an image, adjust a headline, or refine a font without affecting anything else, with every element remaining fully layered and editable throughout.
Video 4
Memory Library turns every interaction into a building block. With persistent memory, Canva AI 2.0 understands how you work, keeps every project on brand, and applies your style automatically. The more you create, the better it knows how you work, and every suggestion gets more useful.
Video 5
Intelligent new workflows
Built on that foundation are six new workflows that extend Canva AI 2.0 across your whole creative process, making Canva the place where teams can start and end their day.
Connectors plug Canva AI directly into the tools and workflows your team already uses. Connect Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Notion, Zoom, HubSpot, Microsoft, Atlassian, and Linear, with more to come, and Canva AI can draw on your conversations, content, and context to create exactly what you need. Generate meeting summaries from Zoom transcripts, turn customer emails into personalised sales pitches, or build a company newsletter from activity across Slack, all as finished, on-brand visual outputs.
Video 6
Scheduling puts your work on autopilot. Set tasks once and Canva AI handles the rest, running automatically in the background, even while you're offline. Whether you’re generating a full batch of social content every Friday, or scanning your emails each morning to create briefing documents for your upcoming meetings, the work is ready when you log in.
Video 7
Web research brings the web into your creative process. Run research on demand or schedule it in the background, and Canva AI gathers and structures information from across the web – from business proposals to market exploration – delivering it directly into your design as structured, editable content.
Video 8
Brand Intelligence ensures every design starts and stays on brand. Connect your brand template or describe what you need, and Canva AI automatically applies your fonts, colours, and style from the first output. You can also instantly update existing work by asking Canva AI to apply your latest brand, turning hours of manual updates into a single step done in seconds.
Video 9
Canva Code 2.0 opens up a whole new kind of design: fully interactive experiences built from a single conversational prompt. Describe what you want and Canva AI builds a complete, responsive experience that works across every device. Now with HTML importing, you can also bring any HTML file or AI-generated experience into Canva and edit it yourself, with no rebuilds required. Add forms that collect responses in Canva Sheets, drop interactive elements into presentations, or publish to your own domain with SSO protection.
Video 10
Sheets AI takes the work out of building spreadsheets from scratch. Describe what you need, from a budget tracker to a project timeline or a content calendar, and Canva AI generates a fully structured, beautifully designed sheet, populated with real data and ready to use.
Image 7: Canva AI helping create a Canva Sheet
Try for yourself
We've always believed that everyone has ideas worth bringing to life. Canva AI 2.0 is our biggest step yet toward making that real – closing the gap between imagination and finished work, without taking away any of the control you'd want along the way.
We can't wait to see what you create with it!
Learn more about Canva AI 2.0 here⁠(opens in a new tab or window). A secret password will be revealed during the Canva Create keynote, and those who find it first will get early access to Canva AI 2.0 and unlock a special gift. General availability rolls out over the coming weeks. T&Cs apply⁠(opens in a new tab or window).

Meet your new creative partner. Canva AI 2.0 brings everything you need together in one place. 
It features nine capabilities that will save you countless hours and transform the way you work.
1. Design through conversation: Simply talk through what you need to turn rough concepts into polished, professional results. 
2. Agentic Orchestration: It can now decide on images, text, fonts, colors, and even layouts on your behalf.
3. Memory Library: Intelligent design that learns from you, and gets smarter and more personal with every project you create.
4. Layered Object Intelligence: Generate fully layered designs where every text box, image, and graphic is editable, so you retain total creative control.
5. Canva AI Connectors: It creates what you need using context from apps you use every day, like Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, or your Calendar.
6. Scheduling: Schedule tasks to run automatically, putting work on autopilot even while you’re offline.
7. Web Research: Let it do the research for you and pull what you need from the web directly into your design.
8. Brand Intelligence: It automatically applies your brand to anything you create, so every design is on-brand by default.
9. Canva Code 2.0: Bring any HTML or code file into Canva, and it becomes fully editable. Add forms that collect responses, interactive designs, and more.
Watch the next video to see how you can use all these features at work or for play.
Want to dive straight in? Explore our latest launches at canva.com/launches

An important update on our team
Today, Canva Co-Founder and CEO Melanie Perkins sent the following note to the Canva team.
Hi everyone,
Today, I have some profoundly difficult news to share.
After months of thinking through how to set Canva up for the next chapter, we have made the incredibly hard decision to make significant changes to how we’re organised, where some of our teams are based, and the roles and skills we need for the future.
This means 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva, will be impacted. For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.
This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history. Behind every decision is someone we care deeply about, and I know the consequences will be very real for those directly affected, their families, friends and teammates.
I’m deeply sorry for the pain and disruption this will cause for everyone affected. While nothing can make this news easier, we will do everything we possibly can to support everyone affected. I want to explain as openly as I can why we're making these changes, how we reached these decisions, and, most importantly, how we will care for the people affected today.
Why we’re making these changes
We've spoken a lot about how quickly the world is changing. New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use.
Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade.
After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I've come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.
It also means making some of the hardest decisions we've ever faced, including saying goodbye to people who have helped make Canva what it is today. For that, I am deeply sorry.
What we’re changing
We're making three changes to bring more of what has made Canva special back into how we work.
1. We're simplifying how we come together to build Canva
As we've grown, more of our work has become organised around team structures and narrow areas of ownership. Improving one part of our product often requires navigating between Product, Growth and Platform, with more handovers and coordination than necessary. This has made it harder to take ownership of bigger problems and to build a deeply unified product for our community. We’ve tried many ways to solve this over the years, but it’s become clear we need to revisit our underlying structure.
To do that, we’re bringing Product, Growth and Platform together into one Product Org and changing the way we work to provide clearer ownership, greater autonomy and flexibility to tackle our most important goals. We want to get back to spending more time building, and less time navigating how work gets done.
2. We’re reducing subspecialisation and collapsing layers to broaden ownership
Over time, we've divided work across more and more subspecialties and teams. While this has helped us build valuable expertise, it's also fragmented ownership and made it harder to see the full picture, with different teams responsible for many pieces of the same work.
We're reducing this fragmentation and incorporating narrower subspecialties into broader roles so teams have more ownership of goals from start to finish. We're also simplifying layers, consolidating overlapping responsibilities, and ensuring teams have the right mix of skills and experience for the chapter ahead.
3. We’re co-locating closely connected teams and increasing in-person collaboration
Working across countries has brought enormous benefits and talent, but it’s also made it harder to bring the right people together to solve complex problems. We’ll continue investing in our global team, particularly where being close to our community, customers and markets matters most.
At the same time, Sydney will become the primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important. We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we're committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support.
We also want to bring more teams together in person to build trust, learn from one another and strengthen the connections that make Canva special. From January, we expect most Hybrid Canvanauts to spend around 2 to 3 days in the office each week, depending on what makes sense in your area.
How we approached these decisions
I know many of you will have questions about how we made these decisions. We began with one question: what does Canva need to do to succeed in the chapter ahead?
We started with our mission and future goals, then considered the structures, skills and locations needed to achieve them. Only then did we look at what this would mean for individual roles. While understanding how we reached these decisions won't make them any less painful, I want to emphasise that they are not a reflection of the talent, care and dedication people have brought to Canva, their skills or the enormous contributions they've made along the way.
Supporting those who are leaving
We know everyone's circumstances are different, and while nothing can make today’s news easy, we've tried to reflect those different needs in the financial, career and wellbeing support we're providing to everyone affected:
We’re also launching the Canva Collective Fund, providing US$10,000 grants to departing Canvanauts who want to start something of their own. Whether it’s starting a business or doing something meaningful for their local community, the fund is designed to help get those ideas off the ground. Everyone leaving as part of these changes will have until the 14 of December to register their interest, and we won’t take any ownership or equity in what they create.
What happens next
Our immediate priority is to make time for the conversations with everyone directly impacted by these changes. Those impacted will receive a calendar invite for an individual meeting with a senior leader in their area to discuss the next steps and support available should they wish to attend.
With teams across 37 countries, we'll need to follow different local requirements and processes, which means the timing and way these conversations happen may vary depending on where people are based.
We also want to give everyone the time to process this news and say goodbye in their own way. Everyone leaving Canva will continue to have access to Slack and Gmail until the end of the week, so they can choose when and how to share the news with their teams. This means you may not know exactly how your team is changing straight away, and we ask everyone to respect the privacy of those having these conversations. Leads will share more about the changes to different areas by the end of the week.
We've put together some answers to common questions and everything you need to know. There's no need to read through everything right now, but we hope they'll be helpful whenever you're ready. Next week, we’ll come together for a Company All Hands on November 10th to talk through these changes, answer questions, and share more about the path ahead. We’ve asked Org Leads to wait until after this to bring their teams together, with Org All Hands taking place from November 11th.
To everyone continuing at Canva: I know this news will be incredibly difficult, especially as we say goodbye to friends and teammates who have been such an important part of our journey. Please look after yourselves and one another and be there for those who are leaving. We’re also cancelling non-critical meetings for the rest of the week, and encourage anyone who needs some time and space to process this news to take the day off. There’s no need to log this as leave.
To those who will be leaving Canva: I wish I could adequately express how grateful I am for everything you've contributed. The Canva that exists today is the result of your hard work, creativity, passion and care. Hundreds of millions of people around the world have been empowered by what you've helped build, and I hope you know just how much of a difference you've made. I am deeply sorry this is how your chapter at Canva is ending. Please know these decisions do not diminish your talent, the value of your contributions, or the difference you've made here. We will do everything we can to support you in what comes next, and I hope the work we do from here will be worthy of what you've helped build.
Mel

For the 2027–2028 cycle, the ANZ summer program (December 2027 start) is expected to open applications around April 2027, while US summer roles (May–August 2028) typically post September through November. That 30-day ANZ window isn't a suggestion: Prosple’s listing documented a late-April open and late-May close for the last cycle, and Reddit users report that positions close when filled, not when the calendar says so.
What Is a Canva Internship?
A Canva internship is a paid, 12-week summer placement that puts penultimate-year students into real product teams at one of the world’s largest private tech companies, valued at $42–65 billion. Interns ship features used by 260 million monthly active users across design, engineering, data, and marketing tracks. The program starts with a one-week onboarding bootcamp and is remote-friendly: "if you want to do work from the office, at home, or a bit of both, it’s completely up to you." Glassdoor rates Canva 3.9 out of 5 from 862 reviews, with intern interviews scoring a 67% positive experience rate. The 37 former interns who transitioned to full-time through Canva’s Launchpad program show the pipeline is real.
When Do Canva Internship Applications Open for 2027–2028?
Canva’s calendar splits across two hemispheres, and the distinction matters more than most applicants realize. The ANZ summer program (December start) opens applications around April, keeps the window live for roughly 30 days, and closes by late May. The US summer program (May–August) posts roles September through November on a rolling basis. For the 2027–2028 cycle, that means the ANZ window is expected around April–May 2027 (about 8 months before the December start), while US roles should appear September–November 2027. The overall interview process runs 4–5 weeks from recruiter call to decision, which is fast by tech standards. One thing to note: Canva has not posted 2027–2028 dates yet, so registering interest via their Early Careers page is the only way to catch the window when it opens.

Why You Must Apply the Week Applications Open
Canva’s official Early Careers page says the internship is a 12-week program for penultimate-year students, and Prosple’s listing documented that "roles will be live for 30 days." Thirty days is the entire window, and review is rolling inside it. Reddit confirms the pattern: one thread notes that applications were still being accepted in mid-May for a recent intake, with the board closing shortly after. Another thread asks if anyone even got the OA, and the answer was mostly rejections. The math is simple: a 30-day window with rolling review means late applicants compete for whatever seats the first two weeks didn’t fill.

The honest answer is the one whose skills you can already show, because each track interviews against its own technical bar. And one common thread runs through all of them: product thinking, the ability to connect your work to outcomes for 260 million users.

What Are the Eligibility Requirements?
Canva publishes the same core requirements across its internship tracks:
• Enrollment: penultimate-year (second-to-last year) tertiary student. Canva’s official early careers page says the program is for "penultimate year tertiary students," and FinalRoundAI reports expected graduation dates of Dec 2026 to Jun 2028 for the current cycle.
• Degree fields: CS, Design, Statistics, or closely related disciplines for engineering and design tracks. Marketing and other tracks have their own requirements.
• Work authorization: Australian work rights required for Sydney and Melbourne roles. US work authorization preferred for Austin and San Francisco. No explicit visa sponsorship language found in any posting.
• Availability: the full 12 weeks. The program is remote-friendly: "if you want to do work from the office, at home, or a bit of both, it’s completely up to you."
Does Canva Have a GPA Cutoff?
No. No GPA requirement appears in any Canva internship posting, FAQ, or careers page. This is verified absence, not omission: Canva’s official how-we-hire page emphasizes skills and product thinking over academic scores, and explicitly says "even if you don’t think you quite meet all of the skills listed or tick all the boxes, we’d still love to hear from you." What actually gates you? Two things. The penultimate-year requirement excludes graduating seniors and first-year students alike. And work-authorization requirements vary by office: Australian work rights for Sydney/Melbourne, US authorization for Austin/SF. Beyond that, Canva screens for product-building experience, technical skills, and alignment with its "Crazy Big Goals" culture.

What Is the Canva Application and Interview Process Like?
Canva’s funnel is structured and runs about 4–5 weeks from recruiter call to decision:
1. Apply at lifeatcanva.com with your resume. You’ll get a confirmation email immediately. About 1–2 weeks later, a recruiter reviews your application and, if successful, arranges a Zoom call.
2. Recruiter Zoom call (20–30 min). Aspirations, experience, and culture fit. Canva calls this the "initial conversation" and says it kicks off the 4–5 week process.
3. Online Assessment (90 min, 3 questions). For backend SWE, this is Java-only with no other language options. ML/AI adds math/stats-heavy MCQs. Reddit consensus: "Hardest part of Canva’s intern process is passing the OA."
4. Technical interview and offer. SWE: LeetCode easy/easy-medium plus system design. ML/AI: 75-minute final (15 min behavioral + 60 min technical coding, AI-assisted). Offers specify team, location, and compensation.
One thing that makes Canva’s process unusual: they explicitly encourage AI use at every stage, including interviews. "Just be ready to explain how you used it, what you kept, changed, or built on." The behavioral portion uses the STARR method (Situation, Task, Action, Results, Reflection), not standard STAR, so practice adding the Reflection step. Glassdoor rates intern interview difficulty 3 out of 5 with an average 22-day process.

How Do You Stand Out When 60 Seats Fill in 30 Days?
Three moves, all executable before April. First, apply in week one of the window. Rolling review plus positions that close when filled makes timing itself a filter. Second, build the evidence Canva actually evaluates: product-thinking projects, AI-assisted development workflow, and portfolio proof that you shipped something. Canva’s interviewers use the STARR method and explicitly ask how you use AI tools, so having a project where you used AI to build, tested the output, and iterated on it's worth more than another LeetCode solve. Third, prepare for the OA like it’s the real gate, because Reddit says it's. For backend, that means Java fluency (no language choice). For ML, it means brushing up on math and stats fundamentals alongside coding. The technical interview after the OA is reportedly easier. And remember what 37 Launchpad conversions tell you: the internship is a 12-week audition for a full-time role.

FAQ
When do Canva internship applications open for 2027–2028?
For the ANZ summer program (December 2027 start), applications typically open in April and stay live for about 30 days, closing in late May. For US summer roles (May–August 2028), postings appear September through November. Canva has not posted 2027–2028 dates yet, so register your interest at lifeatcanva.com/en/early-careers/ and check back early 2027.
Is Canva internship recruiting rolling?
Partially. The ANZ intake has a defined 30-day application window (typically April–May), while US roles reportedly recruit on a rolling basis from September. In both cases, positions close when filled, so applying early within the window gives you the best chance. Reddit users report high rejection rates even at the OA stage.
What GPA or grades do you need for a Canva internship?
Canva doesn't publish a minimum GPA requirement. Their official hiring page emphasizes skills, product thinking, and cultural alignment over academic scores. They explicitly encourage candidates to apply even if they don’t tick all the boxes. Focus on demonstrating product-building experience, technical skills, and alignment with Canva’s Crazy Big Goals culture.
What is the Canva interview process like?
For engineering interns, expect a 90-minute online assessment (3 coding questions, Java-only for backend), followed by a recruiter Zoom call, then a technical interview with LeetCode-style problems and system design. ML/AI adds math-heavy MCQs. The process takes about 4–5 weeks. Canva encourages using AI tools and asks you to explain how you used them.
Do Canva interns get return offers?
Return-offer rates vary significantly by year and market conditions. Third-party estimates put the normal rate around 60%, but during hiring freezes (like 2024–2025), the rate dropped as low as 11% with almost no external grad roles. Canva’s Launchpad program is the primary pipeline from internship to full-time. 37 former interns returned through Launchpad in one cohort.
What skills does Canva look for in interns?
Canva values product thinking across all tracks, the ability to connect technical work to user outcomes for 260 million monthly users. Engineers need Python or Java plus framework experience. ML roles need deep learning and PyTorch. Designers need a portfolio showing product and visual craft. All tracks are evaluated on AI literacy: how you use AI tools, what you kept, changed, or built on.
Are Canva internships paid?
Yes. Australian SWE interns earn approximately A$28–38 per hour (A$61K–79K annualized) with meals provided. US roles reportedly pay $46–60 per hour for SWE, with ML/AI trending higher at $52–60 per hour. US interns receive relocation assistance for Austin and San Francisco. Canva pays 18% above the Australian national average for SWE interns.
Is the Canva backend OA really Java-only?
Yes. Multiple Reddit reports confirm the backend SWE online assessment is Java-only with no other language options. This is a major differentiator versus most tech companies that allow language choice. The OA is 90 minutes for 3 questions at roughly medium difficulty. ML/AI OAs are different: math and stats heavy with both MCQs and coding, and language choice may vary.
The window is 30 days long and the review inside it's rolling. Spend the runway building proof: a remote Externship turns "interested in tech" into a finished AI or product project an April application can point at.

Transcript
[0:00] In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to create an invoice in Canva.
[0:05] First, open your browser and go to canva.com. Then, log into your account. A free account works perfectly for this.
[0:14] One of the best parts about using Canva is that you don't need to design from scratch. There are ready-made invoice templates that you can easily edit,
[0:22] which saves a lot of time and keeps everything looking professional. Once you're in, head to the search bar at the top and type invoice. You'll see a wide
[0:32] variety of styles from simple and minimal to business and freelance focused designs. Take a moment to scroll through and choose a template that fits
[0:41] your brand's tone. If you want to keep cost down, look for designs marked as free. When you found one you like, click
[0:48] it to open the preview. Next, select customize this template. This opens the design in Canvas editor. You'll see
[0:56] placeholders for all the typical invoice elements. Everything on the page, text, colors, and graphics can be adjusted.
[1:04] The interface is drag and drop, so it's very beginner friendly. Now, replace the template text with your information.
[1:12] Click each text box and type in your business name. If you have a logo, we'll add it in a moment. Fill in your client's name and address so the invoice
[1:20] is clearly addressed. Add an invoice number and the date. Using a consistent format helps with your records. In the
[1:28] line item section, list your services or products with clear descriptions, quantities or hours, and individual prices.
[1:36] Check your math as you add the subtotal, tax if applicable, and the total due.
[1:42] Finally, include payment terms or a due date so expectations are clear.
[1:47] Something like due within 14 days or a specific date works well. If you want to personalize the design, you can change
[1:54] colors and fonts to match your brand. To add your logo, go to uploads, select upload files, and choose your logo from
[2:03] your device. Drag it into place and resize as needed. You can also add simple icons or shapes for a touch of style, but keep readability in mind.
[2:13] Make sure there's good contrast between text and background and that the totals stand out. When you're done, it's time
[2:21] to save or send. Click the download button and choose PDF for a clean print ready file. Rename the file with the
[2:30] client's name and invoice number for easy tracking. If you prefer to share digitally, use the share option to send
[2:37] a view only link. You can also keep a copy in your Canva account as a reusable template for future invoices. That's it.
